hero.title: Huawei,
hero.lede: China’s national champion in AI chips and phones, read from its launches, roadmaps and executives’ statements. It answers US controls with products, not press releases.

short_answer.title: It answers with products, on its own calendar
short_answer.body: Big moves land at fixed company events (Huawei Connect in September, HDC in June, the March annual report), so a launch soon after a US move may be coincidence. Every reaction here is still a signal.

short_answer.title: Silence is part of the method
short_answer.body: Huawei does not comment on US rules or confirm how its chips are made; founder Ren Zhengfei plays capability down while rotating chairs claim parity with NVIDIA.

purpose.summary: What Huawei launches, open-sources and claims is in its control, so its record can inform forecasts of China’s domestic answer to US chip controls.
use_for: After a US chip restriction, does Huawei answer with a product, a roadmap or a claim, and how soon?
When NVIDIA loses or regains Chinese buyers, how does Huawei position Ascend?
Will Huawei open-source models and tools to grow its chip ecosystem?
dont_use_for: Chip process or foundry details, which Huawei does not disclose.
Beijing’s purchase guidance, which belongs to the state personas (CAC, MIIT).

standing.class_role: Company · private, employee-owned; China’s leading maker of AI chips (Ascend), phones and telecom equipment. On the US Entity List since 2019.
standing.principal: Its employee shareholding union and board; rotating chairs speak for it, founder Ren Zhengfei on strategy.
standing.attribution_rule: A row is Huawei’s when it comes from the company: launches, annual reports, newsroom statements, rotating chairs and named executives. Ren Zhengfei counts only when he speaks as founder about company strategy.
standing.veto_players: Commerce/BIS (Entity List, foreign direct product rule, the May 2025 Ascend guidance), foundry access (TSMC cut off since 2020; SMIC capacity), and Beijing, whose purchase guidance steers buyers toward Ascend.
standing.gates_held: Supply of Ascend chips and CloudMatrix systems to Chinese AI labs (it served DeepSeek models on Ascend within days, HW11), and the HarmonyOS ecosystem.

powers.use: Ascend chips and CloudMatrix systems for Chinese AI labs
powers.limit: Capped by SMIC process nodes; no advanced foundry access

powers.use: Phones on domestic chips, HarmonyOS, Pangu models
powers.limit: Release dates follow its own event calendar

powers.use: R&D spending of about CNY180-190bn a year
powers.limit: No major outside investments in this log
Does not comment publicly on US rules; the Chinese government answers for it

powers.use: Partners with Chinese labs on Ascend (DeepSeek on Ascend cloud)

powers.limit: No published AI safety framework found in this log
Never confirms chip process or foundry (HW05)
No lawsuit by Huawei in this log

incentives: Sell Ascend hardware; open-sourced software exists to support it
Take China’s AI chip market while NVIDIA is restricted
Show self-reliance to state customers and the party-state
Make up for weak single chips with clusters and in-house memory

positions.position: US controls are the “new normal”: an obstacle to work around, never called effective
Ascend can match or pass NVIDIA in China through clustering
Open-source models and tools to grow the Ascend ecosystem

red_lines: Confirming chip process or foundry details
Any suggestion of post-2020 TSMC manufacturing or model copying
profile.decision_style: Long-horizon and calendar-driven. Rotating chairs give confident roadmaps and NVIDIA comparisons; founder Ren plays capability down to lower US alarm. Quiet launches (the Mate 60 online drop, HW04) and silence (HW05) are used as signals.

relations.note: Ascend is positioned directly against NVIDIA in China
DeepSeek models served on Ascend cloud
Entity List, foreign direct product rule, Ascend guidance

voice.summary: Measured and long-term from rotating chairs; deliberately modest from the founder.

say_do.say: Founder Ren: the US exaggerates Huawei’s achievements; its chips are a generation behind
say_do.do: Rotating chairs claim CloudMatrix beats NVIDIA’s GB200 and that Ascend has passed NVIDIA in China

benchmarks.claim: about 300 PFLOPS vs 180 for GB200 NVL72, at about 4x the power
about 2.8x the FP4 compute of NVIDIA H20

incidents.incident: TSMC-made die reported in an Ascend 910B
Pangu Pro MoE alleged to copy Alibaba’s Qwen 2.5
incidents.what_changed: Flat denial: trained on Ascend, its own work

rules.name: US restriction → self-reliance claim
rules.when: The US tightens chip controls or targets Huawei’s chips
rules.then: Huawei answers weeks to months later with a self-reliance product, roadmap or claim, never with a statement on the rule itself
rules.note: The Mate 60 launch during Raimondo’s 2023 visit (C101 → HW04) is a famous signal but answers a visit, not a restriction, so it is not counted. Counter-case: no verified Huawei statement on the May 2025 guidance itself; MOFCOM answered instead. HW02 is the annual New Year letter, so its timing is calendar-driven.

rules.name: NVIDIA loses Chinese buyers → Ascend push
rules.when: NVIDIA’s access to Chinese buyers is cut (a US licence rule, a CAC summons, a purchase halt)
rules.then: Huawei unveils or pulls forward Ascend products and open-sources its software within days to weeks
rules.note: Confounded by Huawei’s own calendar: HW21 is its annual September conference. The April 2025 CloudMatrix row is month-only, so it cannot count (P1).

rules.name: NVIDIA regains access → head-to-head claims
rules.when: Washington lets NVIDIA sell more to China
rules.then: Huawei compares Ascend directly with NVIDIA’s China parts within weeks
rules.note: Huawei compares against the H20, the China-only part. Ren’s modest framing (HW15) is a counter-case. WAIC (July) and the March partner conference are annual events.

rules.name: Rival open model → Huawei open-sources
rules.when: A Chinese lab releases a major open-weight model
rules.then: Huawei open-sources a Pangu model or Ascend software, framed as ecosystem building
rules.note: No usable episode: Baidu pre-announced the 30 June ERNIE open-sourcing in February (BD08), so Huawei’s same-day Pangu release is not a reaction to it. Kept as a hypothesis to watch.

limits.title: Mostly secondary sources
limits.body: Annual reports and the 2025 keynote were read in the original; most other rows rest on Reuters, Caixin or trade press.

limits.title: Calendar confound
limits.body: Huawei times big moves to fixed events, so a launch soon after a US move is weak evidence of a response.

limits.body: Safety commitments, lobbying records and litigation were not part of this pass.
